changes.after: Include one struct inside another and use its fields.

before: An embedded field uses a type name without a separate field name, such as Address inside Person. The outer value contains that field. Its accessible fields and methods can be promoted for convenient selection.

p.City below means p.Address.City. Person is not automatically an Address subtype. Composite literals still initialize the embedded field explicitly; promoted names are not direct keys in Person{...}.
Expected output or behavior: Rome. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.
Optional local transfer task: Read the same field through p.City and p.Address.City and compare. You may trace it without a Go compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: A Person can contain an Address. Writing just `Address` inside Person embeds it: the field uses its type name as its name.
`p.City` is a shorter way to read `p.Address.City` here. Person contains an Address; it is not itself an Address. When creating the Person, set the Address field explicitly.
The screen shows `Rome`. The shorter path reads the City field inside p.Address.
Both paths read the same field. The shorter path works because Go makes an unambiguous embedded field or method available through the outer value.
